mechanisms.causalChain: A global risk-off shock can reduce foreign portfolio and debt claims, slow FDI, raise offshore rollover costs and pressure FX expectations; those effects reach domestic activity only through exposed borrowers, asset prices, confidence or reserve/intervention channels. SAFE's 2025 external-flow mix is the starting point, not a causal test of Western risk aversion.
mechanisms.counterEvidence: End-June 2026 net external assets remained USD 3.825tn and reserves were USD 3.786tn. External liabilities were 50% direct-investment and 31% portfolio positions; SAFE gross external debt was USD 2.498tn, with 41% of short-term external debt trade-related. IMF reports two-way opening measures and notes the January 2025 easing of cross-border financing macroprudential parameter. These buffers and access changes qualify a simple flight narrative, but do not establish absence of outflows.
mechanisms.stockFlowTransmission: Track BOP transactions by instrument/sector separately from IIP stocks and revaluation. Foreign asset acquisition, liability withdrawal, reserve transactions and net errors must not be netted into one shock scalar. Map FX mismatch and rollover due dates to borrower cash flows; exclude domestic RMB loans from cross-border exposures.
mechanisms.identificationLimits: SAFE H1 BOP aggregates do not identify investor nationality, motive, resident diversification, reserve intervention or valuation. IIP stocks include revaluation; external-debt maturity is original, not remaining maturity. BIS locational banking claims are residence-based and exclude domestic RMB loans. SAFE cross-border receipt/payment turnover is not net capital flow. Control enforcement and circumvention cannot be inferred from formal rules.
mechanisms.modelability: Model as a bounded instrument-specific foreign portfolio/loan/FDI flow shock with borrower exposure and reserve/policy response; do not apply it to all domestic credit.
mechanisms.scenarioRelevance: A global risk-off branch can alter offshore refinancing and confidence, but a current-account surplus and capital controls provide offsets; this is an exposure channel, not the baseline assumption of collapse.
mechanisms.unresolvedUncertainty: Complete H1 2026 sector/maturity BOP table, foreign holder residency by asset, remaining-maturity and FX-mismatch schedules by named borrower, offshore bond/loan redemption calendar, reserve/intervention decomposition, and causal sensitivity to Western risk aversion remain unresolved. The 2025 SAFE broad sector/maturity flow rows are now extracted; they do not identify specific borrowers or motives.
mechanisms.investigationNotes: SAFE's 2026-03-27 release explicitly revises quarterly BOP series since 2019 and adds annual sector/maturity breakdowns; use this vintage instead of the February preliminary release. The revised 2025 data show USD 735.0bn current-account surplus, USD 773.5bn capital/financial-account deficit including reserves and USD 38.5bn positive net errors and omissions. The separate end-2025 IIP reports USD 11.786tn assets, USD 7.715tn liabilities, USD 4.071tn net assets, and USD 3.744tn reserves. These cannot identify private-sector liquidity or risk-off causality. Next investigation should extract monthly SAFE FX settlement and quarterly BIS claims at matched instrument, sector, currency and maturity definitions. SAFE releases now available as of cutoff report H1 2026 BOP, end-June IIP and end-June gross external debt. H1 current-account surplus USD 378.0bn and capital/financial-account deficit USD 345.2bn are aggregate flows; end-June assets/liabilities USD 12.180tn/USD 8.356tn are stocks. SAFE external debt USD 2.498tn includes short-term contractual-original-maturity debt USD 1.469tn, 41% of which SAFE identifies as trade-related credit; bank and other-sector stocks are separated. SAFE’s H1 press transcript records 9.2tn cross-border nonbank receipts/payments (gross turnover) and describes QDII quota/access controls and planned facilitation; gross turnover is not a net flow and planned measures are not enacted. This substantially improves external funding exposure evidence but does not map residency, motives or remaining maturity to domestic obligors. SAFE’s annual USD worksheet (2025 column BY) provides sector/instrument/original-maturity financial-account flows, now archived by cell in extract/safe-bop-2025-selected.csv. In 2025 bank short-/long-term portfolio debt liabilities recorded net decreases USD 53.9bn/USD 45.0bn while resident bank portfolio debt assets increased USD 41.8bn/USD 89.6bn; general-government short-term portfolio debt liabilities fell USD 15.4bn. Direct-investment liability increases were USD 15.0bn financial-sector and USD 65.0bn non-financial. These flows show resident acquisition and foreign liability withdrawal can coexist, but neither institution nor motive is identified at borrower level. SAFE sign convention and original-maturity labels are retained.

mechanisms.causalChain: External funding stress can spill into domestic RMB activity if banks face FX/liquidity pressure, confidence weakens or local borrowers lose refinancing access; PBoC liquidity, deposit funding, state-bank rollover and fiscal transfers can damp that link. Effective loan prices and credit allocation, not LPR alone, govern borrower cash flow.
mechanisms.counterEvidence: PBOC/SCIO reports end-June 2026 social-financing stock RMB 462.06tn (+7.4% y/y), real-economy RMB lending stock RMB 279.16tn (+5.3%), and June weighted-average new corporate-loan rate about 3.0% (down ~20 bps y/y). This counters claims of an aggregate domestic funding shutdown; it does not imply finance reaches weak borrowers or local platforms.
mechanisms.stockFlowTransmission: PBOC household loan/deposit aggregate stocks and H1 net household lending/deposit flows are onshore RMB banking/financial-system data; BIS DSR Q:CN:P is domestic private-sector debt service, not foreign funding. SAFE BOP/IIP/external-debt and BIS LBS remain distinct foreign portfolio/FDI/bank-position measures. Vanke group cash, bank/financial institution borrowings, bonds and Shenzhen Metro related-party loan are issuer consolidated balances; currency and residence categories are not reconciled. LGFV estimates/swap flows are a separate public financing perimeter.
mechanisms.identificationLimits: Stocks, gross flows and service ratios use different dates and coverage. H1 household loan decline does not mean credit stock was written off or that external funding financed the gap. PBOC household aggregates conceal borrower allocation; SAFE gross external liabilities are not matched to local developers or LGFVs. Vanke filing lacks a full residence/currency split.
mechanisms.modelability: Use separate domestic liquidity, credit allocation, realized borrower rate and solvency blocks, with policy refinancing as an explicit contingent offset and credit loss as a separate stock.
mechanisms.scenarioRelevance: In adaptation, bank and fiscal rollover can prevent a foreign funding shock from becoming an economy-wide credit crunch; in severe stress, directed lending may shift losses to banks and public balance sheets rather than extinguish them.
mechanisms.unresolvedUncertainty: Matched resident household/developer/LGFV borrower debt by lender residence, currency, maturity and hedging; latest published national household loan stock beyond Nov-2025; and household-specific debt service remain unavailable. Vanke’s direct issuer primary PDF access requires bypass of its anti-bot challenge or a public exchange copy.
mechanisms.investigationNotes: The September 20, 2026 fixing (latest before the October 20 release) was 3.00% at one year and 3.50% over five years. Treat neither as the policy rate nor actual borrowing cost. IMF 2024 selected issues provides older corporate/LGFV financing composition; it supports the domestic-vs-offshore distinction but cannot calibrate 2026 exposure. PBoC framework page is living and its publication date is undisclosed (publishedAt null in registry). For model work obtain PBoC aggregate financing/loan tables and actual sector effective rates, tagged by observation period and release vintage. PBOC spokesperson data reported through SCIO on 2026-07-15: end-June TSF RMB 462.06tn (+7.4% y/y), real-economy RMB loan balance RMB 279.16tn (+5.3%), government bond balance RMB 101.36tn (+14.2%); H1 net social financing RMB 20.84tn with RMB 10.76tn in real-economy RMB loan additions and RMB 6.44tn net government-bond financing. June weighted-average new corporate and housing-loan rates were about 3.0% and 3.1%. These are macro aggregates and origination averages, not matched LGFV/developer terms. Capital-control investigation found SAFE’s 2023 facilitation notice retains negative-list/end-use rules for capital-account proceeds; SAFE’s July 2026 transcript describes QDII qualification/quota and simplifying reforms while continuing monitoring. Formal rule evidence establishes regulated channels but not effectiveness or actual outflow circumvention. RR0 closure exports BIS DSR Q:CN:P and limits interpretation to private non-financial sector. PBOC end-November-2025 domestic credit/deposit stocks do not substitute for foreign borrowing. Existing SAFE H1-2026 BOP (current account +USD378bn, portfolio -USD151.2bn) and SAFE external debt/IIP data remain flow/position boundaries; PBOC TSF and MOF/IMF LGFV perimeter results remain separate. See household-property-balance-sheet.json for source-linked records and no-addition boundary rules.

mechanisms.causalChain: Lower land-sale revenue and weak project cash generation can reduce local fiscal capacity, impair LGFV debt service, induce refinancing or forced asset sales, and crowd out local investment/services; creditor losses or risk transfer may then affect banks and the central/local fiscal balance. Debt swaps can buy time through term and rate relief.
mechanisms.counterEvidence: The government completed RMB 2tn issuance of 2025 debt-swap bonds and reports lower local interest expense and debt-service pressure; PBOC reports RMB 101.36tn government-bond stock at end-June 2026. Refinancing and transfers can stabilize near-term cash flows, while not reducing consolidated liabilities one-for-one.
mechanisms.stockFlowTransmission: Separate statutory local-government debt, LGFV bonds/loans, guarantees and other contingent liabilities; consolidate intra-public claims. Model annual cash revenue and interest/principal service, refinancing and transfers; a swap changes creditor, maturity and interest but leaves a consolidated liability unless principal is written down or an asset/cash flow repays it.
mechanisms.identificationLimits: IMF 2026 estimates augmented debt 126.6% of GDP in 2025, including LGFVs and government-guided funds; its LGFV debt estimate is 50.9% GDP. These are staff estimates, not an official fully consolidated ledger. MOF swap totals record issuance/program execution, not total hidden liability stock, losses or net debt reduction; local contingent guarantees and creditor cross-holdings are unresolved.
mechanisms.modelability: A range-based local budget and debt-service bridge is feasible; require explicit debt perimeter, cash revenue, maturity profile, transfer response and separate loss allocation. Avoid multiplying IMF augmented debt with reported LGFV debt without consolidation.
mechanisms.scenarioRelevance: A property/land-revenue shock can depress local procurement and investment, but central support or swaps may shift rather than amplify the stress. Scenario severity depends on fiscal incidence and creditor recognition.
mechanisms.unresolvedUncertainty: There is no source-verified locality-by-locality consolidated perimeter with LGFV operating revenues, land/fiscal transfers, interest, maturity calendar, collateral/recovery and cross-guarantees. Debt swap use by instrument and interest cost savings are partly disclosed but the net present value/final loss allocation and private creditor burden-sharing remain unclear.
mechanisms.investigationNotes: The 2025 MOF implementation report documents the debt-swap policy/issuance process; interpret it as refinancing and risk containment, not proof of principal cancellation. IMF 2026 Article IV links property adjustment and local-government finances amid a debt overhang to weak domestic demand and deflationary pressure. IMF 2024 corporate vulnerability estimates use older firm/LGFV coverage. No comprehensive current local cash-flow and consolidated LGFV perimeter is public in this source map; model with explicit bands and no unsupported point estimate. The Ministry of Finance 2026-05-20 implementation report says RMB 2tn 2025 swap-bond issuance was completed and reports lower interest expenses and debt-service pressures without a quantified consolidated loss bridge. IMF 2026 Article IV estimates augmented debt at 126.6% GDP and LGFV debt component at 50.9% GDP for 2025; its definition expands government perimeter to LGFV activity and guided funds. The IMF’s decomposition is a staff estimate and must not be added to MOF hidden debt or official local bonds without checking consolidation. It is a quantitative perimeter estimate, not audited issuer-level coverage.

mechanisms.causalChain: Lower property sales and prices reduce developer presale and financing receipts, constrain completion, impair developer asset values and household housing wealth, and weaken land revenue; lower construction and consumption can then feed back to local budgets and bank collateral/asset quality. Completion guarantees, restructuring and price adjustment can interrupt or redistribute the chain.
mechanisms.counterEvidence: National PBOC household deposit stocks were larger than household loan stocks in the November 2025 aggregate, and H1 2026 household deposits increased while loan flows fell; these aggregates do not establish household balance-sheet weakness. Vanke is a single reviewed, unaudited consolidated group example; national NBS investment/funding flows and IMF augmented LGFV estimates are not stand-alone property-loss observations. Export/secondary-market activity and policy support remain offsets.
mechanisms.stockFlowTransmission: Separate household loan/deposit stocks (PBOC Nov-2025); debt-service ratio (BIS 2026-Q1 composite); H1 2026 household loan/deposit flows; NBS developer investment/sales/funding flows through Aug-2026; and Vanke June-2026 assets/liabilities, inventory write-down and financing. Vanke inventory RMB347.967bn is an accounting asset stock; write-down RMB3.937bn is a six-month impairment flow, not sector-wide property price loss. SAFE BOP/IIP/external debt describe external flows/positions, not the domestic developer liability base. LGFV debt (IMF expanded estimate/MOF swap issuance) is a distinct public perimeter, not additive to the Vanke group balance sheet.
mechanisms.identificationLimits: Vanke report data were exposed through a secondary text mirror after issuer announcement page slider and direct mirror HTTP 403; figures require primary filing validation. A single listed developer cannot represent private/unlisted developers, JVs or all regions. Mortgage-specific stock, arrears and collateral valuation are undisclosed in located aggregate PBOC tables; NBS funding-flow declines do not identify balance-sheet impairment, pre-sale completion costs or foreign creditor exposure.
mechanisms.modelability: A scoped issuer liquidity bridge can compare available cash, restricted deposits, due-within-year principal, current/noncurrent bank borrowings, bonds, inventory, contract liabilities, impairment and related-party borrowing. National simulations must keep household, developer and LGFV perimeters separate; represent missing mortgage and developer stock parameters as bounded assumptions or leave them uncalibrated.
mechanisms.scenarioRelevance: Vanke reviewed statement reports RMB53.08bn cash versus RMB178.86bn one-year debt principal and carries large inventory/contract liabilities, a concrete illustrative refinancing/completion channel. It does not support extrapolation to the sector. Household aggregate credit and liquidity, cross-border finance and LGFV stock estimates provide separate boundary indicators.
mechanisms.unresolvedUncertainty: Direct Vanke primary report PDF retrieval, sector-representative developer balance sheets, household mortgage-specific stock and borrower distribution, household arrears/debt service, presale delivery obligation stock and same-issuer cross-border debt composition remain unresolved. No property valuation loss is inferred from funding flows.
mechanisms.investigationNotes: NBS's February 28, 2026 communiqué gives 2025 comparable growth rates: development investment -17.2%, new starts -20.4%, completions -18.1%, newly built sales area -8.7%, developer domestic loan funding -7.3%, and personal mortgage funding -17.8%. The same source notes previous-year property indicators were revised for methodology/statistical enforcement, so use comparable growth rates and record the vintage. IMF 2026 attributes weak demand/deflation pressures partly to prolonged property adjustment and LG finance. These flow observations support sector stress, not an exact asset loss or default estimate. Latest NBS report available at cutoff (2026-09-16, Jan-August) reports investment -19.9%, new sales area -12.1%, developer domestic loans -33.3%, deposits/advance receipts -14.8%, completed unsold inventory 753.49m sq.m (-1.1%), and second-hand online transaction floor area +10.6% y/y. These facts sharpen the flow/selected-stock picture and show mixed stabilization signals. No asset/liability bridge, presale-completion stock, household equity/debt service or bank loss recognition was publicly extracted; avoid interpreting funding flow declines as a quantified loss. RR0 closure added PBOC Nov-2025 household credit/deposit stock evidence and Vanke 2026-H1 issuer group asset/liability observations located in a secondary text mirror. Vanke issuer index confirms report dated 16-Sep-2026; report text states reviewed, unaudited IAS 34 statements and material going-concern uncertainty. At 30-Jun: cash RMB53.083bn, current borrowings RMB167.249bn, current bonds RMB14.461bn, noncurrent borrowings RMB130.002bn, inventories/contract costs RMB347.967bn, contract liabilities RMB77.553bn; H1 inventory write-down RMB3.937bn. Shenzhen Metro Group related-party loan balance RMB34.1bn (prior Dec RMB30.5bn). Reviewer note: due-within-year principal RMB178.86bn vs cash RMB53.08bn. This is one issuer illustration and does not measure industry-wide asset losses. Link BOP/TSF/LGFV boundaries through SAFE BOP/IIP/external-debt and PBOC TSF/IMF-MOF claims already in this bundle; do not combine perimeter figures.

mechanisms.causalChain: Aging and changing cohort sizes gradually affect labor-force entry/exit, household formation, housing demand, savings composition, pension and health spending, and the tax base; hours, participation, migration, retirement policy and productivity mediate the impact on output and per-capita welfare.
mechanisms.counterEvidence: Higher participation, later retirement, urbanization/migration, education and automation/productivity can offset falling working-age cohort counts. A population stock alone cannot explain current deflation or determine GDP growth.
mechanisms.stockFlowTransmission: Use age-specific population stocks with birth/death/migration and cohort aging; map working-age populations to participation and hours, and older cohorts to pension/health transfers and dissaving/saving patterns. Keep headcount changes distinct from employment and labor productivity.
mechanisms.identificationLimits: Annual communiqué and the 1% population sample use different age bins and methods; projections are conditional and demographic effects on saving and consumption are institution-specific. Aggregate national totals do not measure labor quality or hours.
mechanisms.modelability: A cohort-based range model is feasible if age bands are harmonized and labor participation, retirement, migration and productivity assumptions are explicit; avoid inferring output elasticities from population changes alone.
mechanisms.scenarioRelevance: Demographic headwinds matter over 2026–2030 but are slow-moving baseline constraints; a sudden 2026–27 structural break cannot be inferred from them.
mechanisms.unresolvedUncertainty: Comparable labor-force series by age, retirement reform timing, cohort household formation, migration, automation and productivity offset remain uncertain.
mechanisms.investigationNotes: NBS annual communiqué reports year-end 2025 population 1,404.89m; ages 16–59 851.36m (60.6%), 60+ 323.38m (23.0%). Its note gives 15–59 as 868.75m. The later May 22, 2026 1% sample survey references Nov 1, 2025, estimates total 1,405.45m and ages 15–59 869.87m (61.89%). Preserve the respective age band/vintage; the divergence is not a clean revision. IMF 2026 says aging weighs over the medium term, without treating it as a sufficient explanation of near-term demand weakness.

mechanisms.causalChain: Property losses, uncertain income and weak confidence can raise precautionary saving or debt repair and lower consumption; weak demand may lower goods prices and nominal income, raising real debt burdens where nominal debts are sticky and feeding back into spending. Fiscal transfers, real wage gains, cheaper imports and exports can offset the loop.
mechanisms.counterEvidence: September 2026 CPI was +0.9% y/y and latest September PPI rebounded to +5.0% y/y (+1.2% m/m), so a current generalized consumer- or producer-price decline is contradicted. Yet living-materials PPI was -0.1% y/y; IMF 2026 continues to describe weak domestic demand/deflationary pressure. PBOC reports H1 household credit flow -RMB0.3668tn and household deposits +RMB7.58tn; those flows and the older stock table do not establish household cohort distress or its distribution.
mechanisms.stockFlowTransmission: Separate 2025-11 household credit/deposit stocks, 2026-H1 net loan/deposit flows, and BIS 2026-Q1 private non-financial-sector debt service (19.1% income). H1 flow changes do not measure debt write-offs, asset losses or June-end stocks. Price index channel differs for consumer price, industrial prices and property collateral; Vanke inventory write-down is an issuer-specific accounting flow, not national property wealth loss.
mechanisms.identificationLimits: PBOC household deposits and loans are unmatched aggregates; mortgage-only balances, arrears, rates, liquid asset distributions and marginal spending by distressed owners are not identified. BIS exports only Q:CN:P private non-financial DSR for China, not household-only. September PPI and CPI coexist with IMF deflationary-pressure diagnosis; causal household spending elasticity and latest GDP deflator remain unvalidated.
mechanisms.modelability: A nominal-real debt service and consumption bridge is modelable with explicit debt coverage, price index, income, MPC and fiscal transfer assumptions. Stress assumptions should be ranges, not calibrated point probabilities absent matched household data.
mechanisms.scenarioRelevance: The new September release changes the latest observed industrial-price sign and weakens any assertion of generalized current goods-price deflation. Scenarios should retain narrower weak-consumption/property-collateral channels, with NBS living-materials prices and current IMF assessment as counterweights; no probability is inferred.
mechanisms.unresolvedUncertainty: No verified household-only BIS DSR exists in the exported China row; no current primary published mortgage stock/arrears by cohort, matched deposit-liquidity distribution or latest GDP-deflator row was located. PBOC November 2025 credit/deposit stocks lag the 2026-H1 flow release.
mechanisms.investigationNotes: The 2026 Article IV says property adjustment and local-government spillovers amid debt overhang have led to continued domestic-demand weakness and deflationary pressures; exports have mitigated this. NBS 2025 records retail-sales nominal growth +3.7%, real per-capita income +5.0% and consumption +4.4%. Reused preflight value: September 2026 CPI +0.9% y/y, monthly +0.2%, Jan–Sep +0.9%; some components (food -1.7%, residence -0.3%) were negative. This does not establish broad price-level decline. IMF's 2023 borrower evidence is an explicit counterweight to generalized balance-sheet repair claims; BIS historical work warns that goods-price deflation and asset-price busts have different implications. NBS August 2026 industrial PPI release (published Sep 10; 2025 base) reported aggregate PPI +3.8% y/y and +0.4% m/m, Jan-Aug average +2.0%; consumer-goods PPI was -0.5% y/y. That was the prior-month observation and was superseded as latest by the September release published Oct 14. September CPI remains +0.9% y/y. Positive aggregate producer inflation and CPI coexist with weaker subcomponents and IMF-described deflationary pressure. The latest GDP deflator was not validated in national series, and no household debt-service distribution was found; mechanism remains a conditional risk, not an observed economy-wide debt-deflation loop. RR0 closure: NBS September release published 2026-10-14 supersedes August PPI; aggregate +5.0% y/y and +1.2% m/m, living-materials PPI -0.1% y/y. BIS official topic bulk CSV exported and latest China Q:CN:P DSR is 19.1% of income in 2026-Q1, private non-financial-sector only; China household-only row absent. PBOC national RMB balance sheet latest populated month found Nov-2025: household loans RMB83.363tn; household deposits RMB163.308tn; these do not match persons/borrowers. H1-2026 household-loan net flow -RMB0.3668tn and deposits +RMB7.58tn are not stocks. Direct SCIO English host returned TLS hostname mismatch; existing official source record reused.

mechanisms.causalChain: After a collateral boom, firms may prioritize debt repayment over investment, households reduce borrowing, and banks delay loss recognition; impaired credit allocation and weak nominal demand can prolong repair. Policy recapitalization, write-downs, income support and asset-price stabilization can shorten it. Japan history makes these channels plausible, not inevitable for China.
mechanisms.counterEvidence: IMF's earlier China analysis found no widespread deleveraging by healthy firms/households; current China has capital controls, a large domestic bank/state role, policy space and stronger exports than some historical Japan crisis phases. The 2026 IMF diagnosis recognizes resilience and does not provide a Japan-path forecast.
mechanisms.stockFlowTransmission: Compare matched sectors' debt, net worth, cash flow, nonperforming assets and saving-investment balances over time; separate private deleveraging from transfer of liabilities to government/banks. A decline in debt/GDP can reflect nominal GDP growth or write-offs as well as repayment.
mechanisms.identificationLimits: Cross-country analogy has confounding institutions, demographics, development level, asset-market structure, policy regimes and loss-recognition timing. Japanese episodes and BIS historical samples cannot identify Chinese causal coefficients or scenario probabilities.
mechanisms.modelability: Use as mechanism-comparison and stress-path options—slow repair, decisive restructuring, or policy-supported adaptation—with distinct balance-sheet accounting. Do not transport historical average growth or crisis duration mechanically.
mechanisms.scenarioRelevance: The analogy bounds plausible persistence if property/LGFV losses and weak nominal demand reinforce each other, while highlighting restructuring and policy choices that can interrupt persistence.
mechanisms.unresolvedUncertainty: Comparable private and public borrower balance sheets, loss recognition and restructuring speed, bank forbearance, demographic productivity, China household saving motives and historical cross-country matching remain unresolved.
mechanisms.investigationNotes: BoJ 2001 scholarship examines monetary transmission under balance-sheet adjustment; BIS 2016 estimates a specific Japanese credit-restriction episode and finds policy instruments can spill beyond intended borrowers; BIS 2010 crisis debt-reduction analysis is descriptive and selected. IMF 2026 supports investigating property/LG finance, weak demand and aging. Counterevidence: IMF China 2023 Article IV's Box 4 found no widespread deleveraging among healthy households and firms in then-available data. So the analogy should inform transmission structures and alternative policy branches only, not declare a structural break or irreversible stagnation.
